walkthroughs.body_html:
Immunity, Infection & Response — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Immunity, Infection & Response brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Immunity, Infection & Response.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A secondary immune response is faster because of:
options: More antigens
Memory cells
Fewer pathogens
Increased phagocytes

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and stronger than the primary?
options: Memory cells generated during the primary response can rapidly proliferate and produce large amounts of specific antibody on re-exposure.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
The pathogen becomes weaker after the primary exposure, so the body has an easier job.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Negative feedback stops the body from responding to any internal change.

mcqs.q: What does negative feedback do in homeostasis?
options: It reverses a change in a controlled variable, bringing it back towards the set point.
Negative feedback stops the body from responding to any internal change.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
Negative feedback makes a process get worse or amplifies the change.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Antigen”?
options: Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Lymphocyte that, when activated, divides and differentiates into plasma cells producing antibodies.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Phagocytosis”?
options: Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Antibody”?
options: Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.
Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.
